fields.current: Should community health clinics have to spend 90% of revenue on program services or pay penalties?

evidence.excerpt: Imposes penalties on nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Centers (community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations) that spend less than 90% of revenue on "program services" advancing their charitable purpose, including but not limited to patient services.

fields.explanation: Question restates the official summary.

fields.current: Federally qualified health centers and similar clinics, with tribal clinics exempt, must spend at least 90% of revenue on program services. Any shortfall is paid as a penalty into escrow and returned only if the clinic reaches 90% within five years. The Attorney General sets what counts, starting from IRS tax-form categories.

evidence.excerpt: “Clinic” shall not include federally recognized Indian tribes, tribal organizations, or urban Indian organizations,
Moneys held in the Special Deposit Fund shall be held in escrow for a period of five years,
Clinics could get their money back if they comply with the spending requirements within five years.
This amount will be based on the data reported in the “total program service expenses” figure from line 4e of Part III
The California Attorney General would define in more detail which kinds of expenses are related

fields.explanation: Text covers FQHCs and FQHC look-alikes, excludes tribal and urban Indian organizations, holds penalties in escrow five years, and starts from IRS Form 990 line items with binding AG guidance.
fields.limitations: Refund also requires the clinic to agree to a Department of Public Health spending plan (text 1234.5(a)); DPH may waive the requirement in exceptional circumstances (AG summary). Neither is in our text. 'Similar clinics' means FQHC look-alikes per the text.

fields.current: Certain private nonprofit health clinics would have to spend at least 90 percent of their revenue each year on providing health care services.

evidence.excerpt: A YES vote on this measure means: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would have to spend at least 90 percent of their revenue each year on providing health care services.

fields.explanation: Matches the official YES statement except 'health care clinics' is shortened to 'health clinics'.

evidence.excerpt: These clinics currently report spending an average of about 80 percent of their revenue on providing health care services, though the percent varies across clinics.

fields.explanation: 80 percent average confirmed in two readings.

fields.explanation: Verbatim.

fields.current: A $50 million clinic at 80% would owe $5 million that year. LAO estimates state enforcement costs of low tens of millions of dollars a year, covered by fees on clinics.

evidence.excerpt: The penalty would equal the amount of spending needed to reach the 90 percent minimum.
State enforcement costs would be in the low tens of millions of dollars per year.
The proposition directs the state to cover the costs by charging fees on affected clinics.

fields.explanation: $5 million example is our arithmetic: 90% minus 80% of $50 million. Cost and fee sentences match LAO.
fields.limitations: LAO also notes other uncertain effects on state and local costs if clinics shift spending or close; not reflected.

fields.current: Community health centers that served about 5.3 million patients in 2022, most with low incomes.

evidence.excerpt: Total patients 5,312,677
Income < 100% FPL 53% 12%

fields.explanation: Patient count and majority low income come only from NACHC, a trade association and independent source. Official HRSA page could not be read. LAO gives a clinic count, not a patient count.
fields.proposedText: Community health centers that served about 5.3 million patients in 2022, most with low incomes, according to their national association.
fields.limitations: Rule 9: independent source cannot be sole support. HRSA UDS (official) failed with robots_disallowed. NACHC counts HRSA-funded health centers; Prop 44 also covers look-alikes, so scope may differ slightly.

fields.current: Clinics spend at least 90% of revenue on program services or forfeit the gap.

evidence.excerpt: Clinics could get their money back if they comply with the spending requirements within five years.
If clinics do not comply within five years, the state would keep the money and spend it on clinic workforce programs.

fields.explanation: 'Forfeit the gap' overstates the immediate effect. The gap is paid as a penalty held in escrow and is refundable for five years.
fields.proposedText: Clinics spend at least 90% of revenue on program services or pay the gap as a penalty, refundable if they comply within five years.

fields.current: Supporters' official argument says some clinics spend under half their funding on patient care, and a 90% floor curbs executive spending.

evidence.excerpt: Yet some clinics spend less than half of their funding on patient care and services,
But some clinic CEOs are misusing taxpayer dollars by diverting millions to inflated executive salaries

fields.explanation: Both claims appear in the official argument. 'Curbs executive spending' is a fair summary of the argument's framing.

fields.current: Opponents' official argument calls it poorly drafted and says it would close many clinics serving millions of patients.

evidence.excerpt: Prop. 44 is a dangerous, poorly drafted measure that would threaten care for millions of California patients.
Force thousands of clinics throughout the state to cut back patient services or shut down entirely.
